name: English written in the Shavian alphabet
variety: British English of the Received Pronunciation type. The eSpeak NG voice uses its default English phoneme table ('en', the table of its British English voice en-GB), a non-rhotic accent close to RP with a short front [a] in TRAP. The Shavian alphabet is a script, not a dialect: its reference spellings follow RP, with every historical r written
sources: Shaw, Bernard (1962). Androcles and the Lion. The Shaw Alphabet Edition, with a reading key, notes on the spelling by Peter MacCarthy and suggestions for writing by Kingsley Read. Harmondsworth: Penguin.
MacCarthy, Peter A. D. (1969). The Bernard Shaw alphabet. In Haas (ed.), Alphabets for English. Manchester University Press.
The Unicode Standard, Shavian block (U+10450 to U+1047F).
Roach, Peter (2004). British English: Received Pronunciation. Journal of the International Phonetic Association 34(2), 239-245.
Wells, J. C. (1982). Accents of English. 3 volumes. Cambridge University Press.
Cruttenden, Alan (2014). Gimson's Pronunciation of English. 8th edition. London: Routledge.
Deterding, David (1997). The formants of monophthong vowels in Standard Southern British English pronunciation. Journal of the International Phonetic Association 27, 47-55.
Grabe, Esther and Low, Ee Ling (2002). Durational variability in speech and the Rhythm Class Hypothesis. In Gussenhoven and Warner (eds.), Laboratory Phonology 7. Berlin: Mouton de Gruyter.
Wells, J. C. (2006). English Intonation: An Introduction. Cambridge University Press.

vowel_formants.speaker: mean of five adult male BBC broadcasters, vowels measured in connected speech

contrasts: the alphabet has one letter for each of 24 consonants and 16 vowels and diphthongs, plus 8 compound letters: six for a vowel followed by r (are, or, air, err, array, ear) and two for the sequences in ian and yew
FOOT versus STRUT (letters wool and up) and TRAP versus PALM or BATH (letters ash and ah): the spelling keeps the splits of southern British English
LOT versus THOUGHT (letters on and awe)
schwa has its own letter (ado), so reduced vowels are written as such
historical r is always written, with the compound letters, so the spelling can be read with a rhotic or a non-rhotic accent; the voice reads it non-rhotically
voiced and voiceless consonants are paired letters (tall and deep forms)
allophony: /p t k/ are aspirated at the start of a stressed syllable and unaspirated after /s/
vowels are clipped before voiceless consonants
/l/ is clear before vowels and dark before consonants and pause
/ɹ/ occurs only before vowels; the letters for vowel plus r are read as long vowels or centring diphthongs, with a linking /r/ before a following vowel
final unstressed happY is [i] for most present-day speakers
/uː/ is fronted; /æ/ is an open front [a] for many present-day speakers
unstressed syllables have schwa, [ɪ] or a syllabic consonant; function words have weak forms
/t/ is often a glottal stop before a consonant
phonotactics: /r/ occurs only before a vowel in the accent of the voice
the short vowels need a following consonant in a stressed syllable
/ŋ/ does not begin a syllable; /h/ only begins a syllable
in Shavian text a raised dot before a word marks a proper name, and the words the, of, and, to are written with one letter each

stress.rule: Stress is fixed for each word and is not shown in Shavian spelling; the written vowels help, because unstressed syllables are mostly written with the letters for schwa, the short i and the array letter.
stress.cues: pitch movement on accented syllables, duration, loudness and vowel quality

rhythm.vowel_reduction: strong: most unstressed syllables have schwa, [ɪ], [i] or a syllabic consonant
rhythm.notes: The nPVI value comes from one speaker of Southern British English reading a text.

length.notes: Long and short monophthongs contrast, with differences of quality; the alphabet pairs them as letters (if and eat, wool and ooze).

intonation.declarative: a high head that steps down through the accented syllables, and a falling nuclear tone on the last accented word
intonation.yes_no_question: low rise or high rise on the nucleus; a fall is also common
intonation.continuation: fall-rise or low rise at the end of a non-final phrase
intonation.accent_shape: nuclear fall (H* L); prenuclear accents are high level steps

phonation: glottal reinforcement of syllable-final /p t k tʃ/

problems: word stress is guessed, because the spelling does not show it and the Shavian part of the dictionary has only letter names, 14 short forms and 8 words: begin and example are stressed on the first syllable, and information and understand have primary and secondary stress exchanged
the rules put a primary stress mark on the compound letters are, or, air, err and ear, so every syllable written with them is stressed

function words written in Shavian are not recognised, except the few in the list: it, was, he, can, from, we, at come out stressed and in their strong forms, where the same sentence in Latin letters has weak forms
TRAP is the front [a] of the default British table, and BATH depends on the script: Latin bath gives short [a], while the usual Shavian spelling with the letter ah gives [ɑː]
the letter ian is read as a long [iː] plus schwa
wh-questions get the rising question tune
good: all 48 letters are mapped to phonemes one to one, which the phonemic spelling allows
the naming dot is accepted, and the one-letter words for the, of, and, to, for are in the dictionary with their weak forms
the letters for vowel plus r are read as non-rhotic vowels with a linking r before a vowel (car is, far away)
schwa letters give reduced vowels, so words written with them get their stress by default on the full vowel (about, ago, computer, banana)

notes: The formant and rhythm values are those of Received Pronunciation, repeated from the profile en-gb-x-rp; the default British table of eSpeak NG differs from RP mainly in TRAP.
